abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) cell culture systems are becoming more widely applied to model tissue organization, disease progression, and therapeutic response. Yet, the molecular characteristics that distinguish organoids and spheroids from conventional monolayer culture are incompletely defined. Here, using tumorigenic organoid models of high-grade serous tubo-ovarian cancer (HGSC), we establish a quantitative proteomic resource that reveals how cell architecture and media independently but jointly shape the cellular state in organoids, spheroids, and monolayers. We further pursue HGSC subtype-enriched features within this framework and identify that a poor prognosis-associated genotype with reported paclitaxel hypersensitivity, Trp53-/-;Pten-/-;Nf1-/- (PPN), is marked by increased microtubule-associated proteins, lipid-associated factors, and mitochondrial remodeling. PPN cells displayed clustered lipid droplets, whereby mitochondria-ER tethering increased. Relative to Trp53-/- (P) and a frequent HGSC genotype, Trp53-/-;Brca1+/-;MycOE (PBM), live-cell imaging showed that PPN exhibits the highest degree of stable mitochondria-ER encapsulations, coincident with fission-biased mitochondria and a high-flux respiratory state. Disruption of the mitochondria-ER contact protein PTPIP51 reduced lipid droplet clustering in the PPN state. Because cytomegalovirus is known to exploit host mitochondria remodeling, mitochondria-ER contacts, and metabolic output during infection, we tested whether this pre-existing host configuration is associated with cytomegalovirus permissiveness. PPN organoids exhibited greater murine cytomegalovirus infection and infectious output than matched monolayers or PBM. Together, these data define a resource of distinct protein characteristics between matched monolayer, spheroid, and organoid systems that should be considered for experimental design. We also uncover a mechanistic axis connecting 3D architecture, organelle contacts, metabolism, drug response, and viral permissiveness.
